--- title: "Genotype replacement in R" description: "Estimate how fast a new dengue genotype takes over, with a logistic model fitted to sequence counts." categories: [Dengue, Tutorial] date: 2026-10-24 image: ../assets/img/dengue.svg image-alt: "Illustration of dengue genotypes replacing one another over time" open-graph: image: ../assets/img/card-genotype-replacement.png image-alt: "Genotype replacement in R, a tutorial by Rhys Inward, with an illustration of genotypes replacing one another" twitter-card: image: ../assets/img/card-genotype-replacement.png image-alt: "Genotype replacement in R, a tutorial by Rhys Inward, with an illustration of genotypes replacing one another" card-style: summary_large_image --- When a new genotype arrives, the share of sequences that belong to it often follows an S-shaped curve. A logistic model fitted to monthly sequence counts sums up the takeover in one number: how fast the odds of sampling the new genotype grow each month. This tutorial uses simulated data, so you can check that the model recovers a known answer. You'll need **dplyr** and **ggplot2**. ## 1. Simulate sequence counts Three years of monthly sequencing, about 40 sequences a month, with the new genotype reaching half of all sequences in month 18. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) set.seed(42) months <- 0:35 true_growth <- 0.25 seqs <- tibble( month = months, n = rpois(length(months), 40), new = rbinom(length(months), n, plogis(true_growth * (months - 18))), old = n - new ) head(seqs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 4 month n new old 1 0 48 0 48 2 1 36 0 36 3 2 40 0 40 4 3 33 0 33 5 4 39 0 39 6 5 49 2 47 ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Plot the raw proportions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(seqs, aes(month, new / n)) + geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#B2433A", alpha = 0.75) + scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, guide = "none") + labs(x = "Month", y = "Proportion new genotype") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Share of sequences belonging to the new genotype each month. Point size shows the number of sequences.](genotype-replacement_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of the monthly share of sequences that belong to the new genotype over 36 months. The share stays close to 0 for the first six months, passes one half around month 18 and is close to 1 by month 30. Larger points mark months with more sequences.' width=672} ::: ::: ## 3. Fit a logistic model A binomial GLM with month as the only predictor. The slope is the growth rate on the log-odds scale. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- glm(cbind(new, old) ~ month, family = binomial, data = seqs) coef(summary(fit)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -4.5876913 0.23203198 -19.77181 5.207782e-87 month 0.2516952 0.01222148 20.59449 3.075353e-94 ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Plot the fit ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pred <- predict(fit, se.fit = TRUE) seqs <- seqs |> mutate( fit = plogis(pred$fit), lo = plogis(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit), hi = plogis(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit) ) ggplot(seqs, aes(month)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#B2433A", alpha = 0.18) + geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "#B2433A", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(aes(y = new / n, size = n), colour = "#1D2930", alpha = 0.55) + scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, guide = "none") + labs(x = "Month", y = "Proportion new genotype") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fitted logistic curve with a 95% confidence interval.](genotype-replacement_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='The same monthly proportions with a fitted S-shaped logistic curve rising from near 0 to near 1, crossing one half around month 18, inside a narrow shaded 95% confidence band that follows the points closely.' width=672} ::: ::: ## 5. Read off the growth advantage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} growth <- coef(fit)[["month"]] c(growth = growth, odds_ratio_per_month = exp(growth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` growth odds_ratio_per_month 0.2516952 1.2862039 ``` ::: ::: The model estimates a growth rate of 0.25 per month against a true value of 0.25. Each month, the odds that a sequence belongs to the new genotype multiply by about 1.29. ## 6. Try it yourself The same simulation and model, running in your browser: three years of monthly sequencing, with the new genotype reaching half of all cases in month 18. Change a setting and the sequences are drawn again and the model refitted. Things to try: - **Sequence the new genotype more often.** Choose *3 times as often*. The new genotype looks commoner than it is and the curve shifts earlier, but the growth rate barely moves: a bias that stays constant shifts the curve without changing its slope. - **Sequence it more often early on only.** Choose *More often early on*. The first months look further along than they are, the curve flattens, and the growth rate drops to about 0.21 against a true 0.25. - **Sequence less.** Drop to 5 sequences a month. The estimate still centres on the truth, but its confidence interval is about three times wider. ```{ojs} //| echo: false import { simulateSequences, logisticFit, labelRange, tidyPlot } from "./explorers.js" ``` ::: {.explorer .ex-geno} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof growth = labelRange(Inputs.range([0.05, 0.6], { value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "True growth rate (per month)" })) viewof perMonth = labelRange(Inputs.range([5, 200], { value: 40, step: 5, label: "Sequences a month" })) viewof sampling = Inputs.radio(new Map([ ["At random", "random"], ["New genotype sequenced 3 times as often", "constant"], ["More often early on, fading by month 18", "fading"] ]), { value: "random", label: "Which cases get sequenced" }) viewof seed = Inputs.button("New random sample", { value: 4, reduce: v => v + 1 }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false biases = ({ random: () => 1, constant: () => 3, fading: m => 1 + 2 * Math.max(0, 1 - m / 18) }) seqs = { const lcg = d3.randomLcg(seed); return simulateSequences({ growth, perMonth, bias: biases[sampling], rpois: d3.randomPoisson.source(lcg), rbinom: d3.randomBinomial.source(lcg) }); } fit = logisticFit(seqs.map(d => d.month), seqs.map(d => d.newer), seqs.map(d => d.n)) curve = d3.range(0, 35.01, 0.25).map(m => { const eta = fit.b0 + fit.b1 * m; const se = Math.sqrt(fit.cov[0][0] + 2 * m * fit.cov[0][1] + m * m * fit.cov[1][1]); const p = x => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-x)); return { month: m, fit: p(eta), lo: p(eta - 1.96 * se), hi: p(eta + 1.96 * se), truth: p(growth * (m - 18)) }; }) fitted = Number.isFinite(fit.b1) && Number.isFinite(fit.se1) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`

Share of sequences each monthFitted curve and 95% intervalTrue share of cases

` ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false tidyPlot(Plot.plot({ width, height: 250, marginLeft: 44, marginBottom: 36, ariaLabel: "Share of sequences belonging to the new genotype, with the fitted and true curves", ariaDescription: `Monthly share of sequences that belong to the new genotype over 36 months, with a fitted logistic curve${fitted ? ` growing at ${fit.b1.toFixed(2)} per month` : ""} and the true curve, dashed, growing at ${growth.toFixed(2)} per month.`, x: { label: "Month", domain: [0, 35] }, y: { label: "Proportion new genotype", grid: true, domain: [0, 1] }, r: { range: [1.5, 5] }, marks: [ fitted ? Plot.areaY(curve, { x: "month", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: "currentColor", ariaDescription: "fit band" }) : null, Plot.dot(seqs.filter(d => d.n > 0), { x: "month", y: d => d.newer / d.n, r: "n", fill: "currentColor", ariaDescription: "points" }), fitted ? Plot.lineY(curve, { x: "month", y: "fit", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2, ariaDescription: "fit" }) : null, Plot.lineY(curve, { x: "month", y: "truth", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "5,4", ariaDescription: "truth" }) ] })) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`

${fitted ? html`Estimated growth rate ${fit.b1.toFixed(2)} per month (95% CI ${(fit.b1 - 1.96 * fit.se1).toFixed(2)} to ${(fit.b1 + 1.96 * fit.se1).toFixed(2)}), against a true ${growth.toFixed(2)}.${fit.b1 > 0 ? ` The odds of sampling the new genotype double every ${(Math.LN2 / fit.b1).toFixed(1)} months.` : ""}` : "The model could not be fitted to this sample. Try more sequences a month."}

` ``` ::: Your browser draws its own random numbers, so these samples differ from the one above, which R generated with `set.seed(42)`. The sampling choices are illustrations, not real data. ::: {.callout-note} ## With real data Sequencing is rarely random. Check how samples were chosen for sequencing before reading the slope as a fitness advantage, and if you pool several places, consider a random effect for location. :::
